sample_test_cases.explanation: The linked list is reversed by changing the direction of every pointer.

hints: You only need three pointers.
Keep track of the previous node while traversing.
Store the next node before changing any links.
Reverse one pointer at a time.
explanation: Traverse the linked list while maintaining three pointers: prev, curr, and next. For each node, save the next node, reverse the current node's pointer to point to the previous node, then move all pointers one step forward. title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: You are given the heads of two sorted singly linked lists list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted linked list and return its head. The merged list should be formed by splicing together the nodes of the original lists.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each list <= 50000
Both linked lists are sorted in non-decreasing order

sample_test_cases.explanation: The two sorted lists are merged while preserving sorted order.

hints: Since both lists are already sorted, always choose the smaller current node.
A dummy node can simplify handling the head of the merged list.
Move the pointer forward in the list from which a node was selected.
When one list ends, append the remaining nodes from the other list.
explanation: Create a dummy node to serve as the starting point of the merged list. Compare the current nodes of both lists and attach the smaller node to the merged list. Move the corresponding pointer forward and continue until one list is exhausted. Finally, attach any remaining nodes from the other list. The algorithm processes each node exactly once, resulting in O(n + m) time complexity and O(1) extra space.

title: Middle of the Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The middle node is 3. Return the linked list starting from node 3.

hints: Counting all nodes first works, but requires two traversals.
Can you find the middle in a single traversal?
Use two pointers moving at different speeds.
When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer will be at the middle.
explanation: Use two pointers: slow and fast. Initialize both at the head. Move slow one step at a time and fast two steps at a time. When fast reaches the end of the list (or can no longer move two steps), slow will be positioned at the middle node. For even-length lists, this naturally returns the second middle node as required. The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The 2nd node from the end is 4, so it is removed.

hints: A two-pass solution is possible by first counting the nodes.
Can you solve it in one pass?
Maintain a fixed gap of n nodes between two pointers.
When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer will be just before the node to remove.
explanation: Use a dummy node before the head to simplify edge cases. Move a fast pointer n+1 steps ahead. Then move both fast and slow pointers together until the fast pointer reaches the end. At this point, the slow pointer will be positioned just before the node that must be removed. Update the links to skip that node and return the modified list. This approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Linked List Cycle
description: Given the head of a linked list, determine whether the linked list contains a cycle. A cycle exists if some node in the list can be reached again by continuously following the next pointer. Return true if there is a cycle; otherwise, return false.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The tail connects to the node at index 1, forming a cycle.

hints: Using a HashSet works, but requires extra memory.
Can you detect a cycle using only pointers?
Use two pointers moving at different speeds.
If a cycle exists, the fast pointer will eventually meet the slow pointer.
explanation: Use Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare). Maintain two pointers: slow moves one step at a time, while fast moves two steps at a time. If the linked list contains a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch up to the slow pointer and they will meet. If the fast pointer reaches the end of the list, no cycle exists. This solution runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Palindrome Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if the linked list is a palindrome, and false otherwise. A palindrome reads the same forward and backward.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The sequence reads the same from left to right and right to left.

hints: Comparing values from both ends is difficult in a singly linked list.
Find the middle of the linked list first.
Reverse the second half of the list.
Compare nodes from the first half and the reversed second half.
explanation: Use the fast and slow pointer technique to find the middle of the linked list. Reverse the second half of the list in-place. Then compare corresponding nodes from the beginning of the first half and the beginning of the reversed second half. If all values match, the list is a palindrome. This approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Reorder List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list L0 → L1 → ... → Ln-1 → Ln, reorder the list to the form L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → ... . You may not modify the values in the nodes. Only the links between nodes may be changed.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Take the last node and place it after the first node, then continue inward.

hints: The last node must come immediately after the first node.
Accessing the last node repeatedly would be inefficient.
Split the list into two halves.
Reverse the second half and merge the two halves alternately.
explanation: First find the middle of the linked list using the slow and fast pointer technique. Split the list into two halves. Reverse the second half in-place. Then merge the first half and the reversed second half by alternating nodes from each list. This produces the required order in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Add Two Numbers
description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, and each node contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list in the same reverse order. You may assume the two numbers do not contain leading zeros except for the number 0 itself.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in each list <= 100000
The represented number does not have leading zeros

sample_test_cases.explanation: 342 + 465 = 807, so the result is represented as 7 -> 0 -> 8.

hints: Process both linked lists digit by digit.
Keep track of any carry generated during addition.
The lists may have different lengths.
Don't forget to create a final node if a carry remains after processing all digits.
explanation: Traverse both linked lists simultaneously while maintaining a carry value. At each step, add the current digits from both lists along with the carry. Create a new node containing the ones digit of the sum and update the carry with the tens digit. Continue until both lists are exhausted and no carry remains. A dummy node can simplify result construction. This approach runs in O(max(n, m)) time and O(max(n, m)) space for the output list.

title: LRU Cache
description: Design and implement a data structure for a Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache. Implement the LRUCache class with the following operations: get(key) and put(key, value). The cache has a fixed capacity. When the capacity is exceeded, the least recently used item must be removed. Both operations must run in O(1) average time complexity.
constraints: At most 200000 operations will be performed

sample_test_cases.explanation: When capacity is exceeded, the least recently used key is evicted.

hints: Finding the least recently used item by scanning all entries is too slow.
You need O(1) access by key and O(1) updates to usage order.
A HashMap can provide O(1) lookup.
A Doubly Linked List can maintain the usage order efficiently.
explanation: Use a HashMap to map keys to nodes in a Doubly Linked List. The linked list maintains the usage order, with the most recently used item near the front and the least recently used item near the back. Whenever an item is accessed or updated, move it to the front. When the cache exceeds its capacity, remove the node at the back of the list and delete its entry from the HashMap. This combination ensures both get() and put() operations run in O(1) average time.
